judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for a plain Blazor component request
judgeRationales.rationale: Both implementations successfully deliver reusable Blazor confirmation dialogs using only built-in APIs. Response A provides a more robust implementation with proper button state management (isBusy flag) to prevent multiple submissions during async operations, which is a critical pattern for production components. A has the core form and service but uses a manual error div and does not clear errors when the email changes, missing two central requirements.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Isolate two static SSR forms on one page
judgeRationales.rationale: Both target the requested separation, but B cleanly implements the canonical static Blazor SSR multi-form pattern with explicit form identities and per-form binding. A's alternate Razor Pages solution may work, yet the evidence shows a more error-prone refactor and incomplete verification signals.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Multi-step booking form with cross-field validation
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Prevent duplicate checkout submission
judgeRationales.rationale: Both build and satisfy the core async submission protections. B is modestly stronger in the user-facing failure experience; A is otherwise comparably complete but uses raw exception text and an unnecessarily restrictive duplicate-address service rule.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for a read-only component
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are correct, display-only ProductCard implementations. B is modestly stronger because its callback carries the selected card data and it handles an absent image with a display-only fallback; A is otherwise fully responsive to the task.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Submit a static SSR contact form
judgeRationales.rationale: B implements the intended static SSR form-binding lifecycle, validation, and confirmation. A has a superficially similar model and markup but fundamentally depends on Blazor event callbacks without an interactive render mode, making the required POST behavior nonfunctional.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Upload a bounded document interactively
judgeRationales.rationale: B delivers the substantially more functional interactive upload page: it uses the appropriate InputFile mechanism and supports the validation/submission workflow. Its MemoryStream-based stub is a meaningful violation of the streaming/no-buffer requirement, so the advantage is limited rather than large. A avoids that buffering in its stub but has a fundamental runtime file-selection defect that makes the core page unusable.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Exclude an HttpContext page from global interactive routing
judgeRationales.rationale: A misses the specified component-routing mechanism, but provides a compiling, request-bound Razor Page at `/download` whose handler inspects headers and writes the file response outside a circuit. B correctly adds the exclusion marker and compiles, but omits the essential conditional global render mode and moves the actual download response to `/download-file`, leaving the stated `/download` static-rendering guarantee unfulfilled.

B's core browser implementation is an explicit simulated 85% reading, not a browser implementation, and it invokes the service during initialization/prerendering. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Auto-saving notepad that survives page reloads
judgeRationales.rationale: B follows the required Blazor/JS interop lifecycle and architecture and correctly owns listener/timer cleanup in the JS module. It has notable functional defects (manual save/clear do not reset the JS unsaved flag, and its timestamp persistence is weak), but A is substantially less viable: it performs JS interop during prerender-unsafe initialization, never wires its OnContentChanged method to the textarea binding, uses a .NET rather than JS autosave timer, and lacks disconnected-circuit-safe disposal.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Focus a validated field without string ids
judgeRationales.rationale: Both implementations miss the central requirement of reliably deferring focus requests made before first render. B is nevertheless the more robust overall implementation: it has a clear typed module wrapper, cached module access, awaited void interop, and server-safe disposal. A's module gate is preferable for pre-render timing but its attempted deferral is not reliable and its disposal lacks disconnection handling.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Infinite scroll list using IntersectionObserver
judgeRationales.rationale: B meets the required .razor.js colocation and correctly uses ChildContent, so the requested body-template usage works; it also handles a HasMore transition by stopping observation. Both still miss important lifecycle requirements (disposed DotNetObjectReference, JSDisconnectedException handling, and InvokeAsync(StateHasChanged)), so the quality advantage is real but not large.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Monitor clipboard changes from JavaScript
judgeRationales.rationale: B implements the central callback/UI-thread and server-disconnect patterns correctly, with a robust collocated module and listener cleanup. Its incorrect DotNetObjectReference disposal cast is a material leak, but A has the more fundamental callback-threading flaw and fragile circuit-handler access.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Responsive layout that adapts to screen size
judgeRationales.rationale: B has the stronger lifecycle and resource-management implementation: a collocated module, explicit JS cleanup, and JSDisconnectedException safety. A better matches the requested raw resize-event mechanism and has a correct CascadingParameter example, but its non-collocated JS and especially its permanent anonymous resize listener are meaningful production defects. B's incorrect final injection example and generic namespace are drawbacks, so the overall advantage is slight rather than large.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for CSS-only responsiveness
judgeRationales.rationale: Both satisfy the requested CSS-only approach. B provides a completed runnable HTML card-grid example in the otherwise empty workspace and clearly summarizes its use; its inclusive 768px breakpoint is a minor precision issue. A's breakpoint is exact and its CSS is sound, but it primarily asks for clarification rather than delivering an artifact.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Update a chart after parameters change
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly implements the key requested architecture: parameter change flagging, post-render interop, and a typed wrapper with centralized disposal. A does reuse and destroy its chart, but misses two central requirements—parameter-change marking and typed interop encapsulation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: User activity tracker that detects idle timeout
judgeRationales.rationale: B meets the central Blazor interop and lifecycle requirements: collocated module naming, retained/disposed DotNetObjectReference, and JSDisconnectedException handling. A does include `keydown`, but its noncollocated module and undisposed callback reference are substantial requirement failures.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wrap a map widget with deterministic cleanup
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses provide functionally identical CSS media query solutions that correctly meet all three rubric criteria. The CSS code is essentially the same (using grid-template-columns: repeat(4, minmax(0, 1fr)) for 4 columns, switching to 1fr below 768px). Response B shows slightly better diagnostic work by identifying the SKILL.md file and providing a helpful comment in the code, while Response A has marginally clearer final wording. These minor differences in presentation and diagnostics do not constitute a meaningful quality difference in the actual solution provided, which is what matters for this CSS-only task."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Update a chart after parameters change
judgeRationales.rationale: Both implementations successfully meet the core task requirements, but Response A is slightly better due to superior architectural design. A's object-reference pattern (where createChart returns a managed object reference) is more robust than B's module-level singleton state, particularly for scenarios with multiple component instances. While B has a marginal advantage in explicit constant naming for better encapsulation, A's two-class wrapper pattern provides good separation of concerns. The architectural difference makes A more suitable for production use where the code might need to support multiple concurrent SalesChart components."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Apply a claim-based authorization policy
judgeRationales.rationale: Both implementations meet all requested authorization, UI, and development-claims requirements, build successfully, and exercise the authorized route under sample Finance-role claims.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Authorize both an Auto page and its API
judgeRationales.rationale: Both solutions protect the API and apply the requested authorization. B is markedly more robust because it relies on the supported Blazor auth-state handoff with all claims serialized and follows the client-side interactive flow; A's custom claim serialization is demonstrably lossy for common claim types and its client HTTP abstraction is not evidenced. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Implement a mutable authentication state provider
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: tie, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Login and account management in a globally interactive app
judgeRationales.rationale: B implements the core architectural fix demanded by the task: excluded auth routes paired with App.razor render-mode selection via AcceptsInteractiveRouting, while preserving InteractiveServer for ordinary pages. A has usable endpoint-based auth plumbing but leaves the app globally interactive and substitutes RenderMode.None rather than the specified exclusion/routing solution, a central functional gap.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Multi-tier app with WebAssembly auth
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: tie, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for non-auth shared state
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Verify per-page Identity endpoints stay static
judgeRationales.rationale: Both miss the requested existing ExcludeFromInteractiveRouting detail, so neither is fully complete. A nonetheless supplies the more useful and specific explanation of the existing authorization redirect and logout request endpoint; B is more precise about per-page rendering but is less complete on routing.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Global logistics tracking for worldwide users
judgeRationales.rationale: B gets the essential rendering-mode recommendation and the latency rationale right, which are central to the task. However, both are materially incomplete on the prescribed two-project setup, Program.cs registrations, and explicit HTTP/matching service registration; A is somewhat stronger only in its initial client/server separation.

judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Mixed storefront with low-latency configurator
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Offline field inspection application
judgeRationales.rationale: Both provide the correct command and broadly sound offline-first WebAssembly design. B is slightly better overall because its architecture is more complete and practical, including explicit queue semantics, retries/backoff, idempotent API operations, and photo-upload handling. Neither explicitly calls out adding a service worker beyond the template, so both share that important omission.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Public news site with one live election widget
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses are strong and give valid commands plus appropriate architectures. B is marginally clearer and more exact about Static SSR versus InteractiveServer, while A has minor imprecision in its framing and scaling explanation.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Recipe community with interactive ratings on static pages
judgeRationales.rationale: Both provide a valid Server-interactivity creation command and broadly appropriate layout. B is more complete, uses the standard generated project placement, and better documents feature roles, although its suggestion to render the full recipe detail page interactively is an avoidable conflict with the desired component-level opt-in. Thus its advantage is modest.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Staff portal with individual accounts
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: tie, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for an existing app feature
judgeRationales.rationale: A actually implements and integrates the requested reusable sortable component and provides build/runtime evidence. B's final claim describes an already-present implementation but its trajectory contains no edits, so it does not substantively execute the requested feature work.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: University course catalog with enrollment form
judgeRationales.rationale: B selects the required noninteractive Static SSR template and explains why it fits, while still providing a complete architecture. A's otherwise reasonable feature plan is built on the wrong interactive Server template, conflicting with the key configuration and rendering requirements.

B has the cleaner no-ID surface and a useful typed wrapper, but A more thoroughly handles focus requests during module initialization and disposal races, with end-to-end coverage of the required lifecycle scenarios.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Infinite scroll list using IntersectionObserver
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are otherwise complete, tested IntersectionObserver implementations with cleanup and generic templating. B more faithfully meets two explicit lifecycle/concurrency requirements: it avoids observing when HasMore is false and marshals JS callback state changes through InvokeAsync. A's guards prevent erroneous loads, so the overall gap is meaningful but not overwhelming.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Monitor clipboard changes from JavaScript
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Responsive layout that adapts to screen size
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are complete, build-clean implementations that satisfy the requested behavior and lifecycle/disposal requirements. B has a modest robustness advantage: its JS watcher map supports multiple provider instances, its cleanup is explicit via AbortController, and its callback marshals the state mutation itself onto InvokeAsync.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for CSS-only responsiveness
judgeRationales.rationale: Both solutions are correct and directly usable. B is marginally stronger because it includes equally correct CSS plus concise integration guidance and a clearer justification for excluding browser/interop callback infrastructure.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Update a chart after parameters change
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: User activity tracker that detects idle timeout
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Wrap a map widget with deterministic cleanup
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are strong, build-clean implementations meeting the core requirements; A has stronger end-to-end browser verification. B is slightly better architecturally and for Blazor lifecycle/circuit safety, using a typed wrapper and deferring parameter-triggered interop to OnAfterRenderAsync.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Apply a claim-based authorization policy
judgeRationales.rationale: Both implementations successfully meet all three rubric criteria with correct policy definitions, route enforcement, and conditional UI. However, Response A is slightly better due to superior validation: it includes explicit runtime verification with curl tests confirming both the protected route renders and the conditional button appears, while Response B only verified the build. Response A also properly configured the authentication/authorization middleware, which is important for the interactive server scenario. Response A demonstrates more thorough testing and a more complete implementation overall, though both would be functionally correct for the stated requirements."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Multi-tier app with WebAssembly auth
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B is significantly better than Response A. The most critical difference is that Response B explicitly configures AddAuthenticationStateSerialization(options => options.SerializeAllClaims = true), which is essential for ensuring role claims are included in the serialized auth state sent to the WASM runtime. Without this configuration (as in Response A), role claims risk being omitted from serialization, causing roles to be lost when the WebAssembly runtime takes over - a fundamental failure of the task requirements. Additionally, Response B uses more idiomatic Blazor patterns with page-level [Authorize] attributes and modifies Routes.razor to use AuthorizeRouteView for comprehensive routing-level authorization. Response A's approach without SerializeAllClaims is a critical oversight that violates the core requirement of maintaining auth state through the WASM handoff." [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Protect an interactive server admin area
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Redirect anonymous users without looping
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A provides a complete, functional end-to-end authentication implementation with proper form submission handling, server-side sign-in, and return URL validation. It successfully demonstrates the behavior by actually allowing users to log in and be redirected. Response B implements the framework correctly in some areas (especially conditional interactivity) but has a critical gap: no POST handler to process login forms and authenticate users. This makes it incomplete and non-functional as a working auth system. While Response B has a slight edge on the render mode criterion, the completeness and functionality of Response A's implementation (allowing actual login flow, handling return URL with validation, including antiforgery) makes it the better overall solution for the stated task."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for non-auth shared state
judgeRationales.rationale: Both Response A and Response B failed to complete the task. While Response A demonstrated more investigative effort by searching multiple directories and discovering actual Blazor projects, it still failed to leverage that information to implement the required theme service. Response B failed more quickly with less investigation. However, since both responses ultimately delivered zero working implementation and no usable code, they are effectively equivalent in terms of final quality and task completion. Neither response met any of the rubric criteria."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Verify per-page Identity endpoints stay static
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B provided a more comprehensive and technically detailed analysis with specific file references, line numbers, and more thorough routing explanation. While both responses correctly verified the account flow without modifying files and met all core requirements, Response B demonstrated superior understanding through more precise documentation of the implementation details (specifically the ExcludeFromInteractiveRouting location and the logout endpoint implementation). Response B's use of the configure-auth skill showed deeper engagement with the task, and its output contained more granular technical information that would be more helpful for understanding the template's design. The difference is not large since both responses are fundamentally correct and fulfill the task requirements, but Response B's additional detail and precision make it the better response."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Exclude an HttpContext page from global interactive routing
judgeRationales.rationale: B implements the required Blazor routing/render-mode pattern and uses HttpContext only for the static excluded page. A solves a different design: an interactive header page plus separate download endpoints, violating the central requirement that navigation to `/download` itself leave the circuit.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Keep a client-only service optional during prerender
judgeRationales.rationale: B provides the requested IBrowserBatteryService contract, a coherent JS-interop browser implementation, explicit server fallback, and post-interactive behavior. A's work is substantially inconsistent: it uses the wrong interface name, creates duplicate/incompatible contract types across projects, adds an unwanted server implementation, and starts/uses the browser service at the wrong lifecycle stage.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Notifications page with live polling
judgeRationales.rationale: B correctly handles the essential prerender-to-interactive state handoff and explicitly gates polling on interactivity, while retaining proper async cancellation/disposal. A's missing persistence violates a central constraint and causes the initial service load to occur twice.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Persist repeated component instances independently
judgeRationales.rationale: B implements the central prerendering requirement with per-store persistent state and conditional restoration, while A implements only in-memory lifecycle caching and thus misses the required hydration handoff and duplicate-fetch prevention. Both otherwise cover the page, model/service/DI, and keyed reordering.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve Auto profile data across activation
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Start a live connection only after activation

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for a static SSR page
judgeRationales.rationale: A delivers a coherent, tested static SSR solution that matches the requested no-handoff architecture. B's InteractiveServer configuration is a central architectural violation and makes its claims about static-only rendering unreliable.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Supply a client service during WebAssembly prerendering
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Implement a mutable authentication state provider
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A is slightly better because it implements a complete, production-ready solution with both development and non-development providers registered in Program.cs. Response B has a functional implementation for development but lacks the critical fallback provider registration for non-development environments, which violates criterion 1's requirement to properly register the AuthenticationStateProvider. Both handle claims building and notification equally well, but Response A's production-safe architecture and AnonymousAuthenticationStateProvider fallback give it a meaningful edge."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Protect an interactive server admin area
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A is significantly better because it fully complies with all four rubric criteria, while Response B violates the critical fourth criterion by using HttpContext in an interactive component (App.razor). Additionally, Response A provides better architectural separation with explicit CascadingAuthenticationState scoping and dedicated components for different auth states. While Response B builds cleanly without warnings, this does not outweigh the rubric violation and architectural issues. Response A's minor build warning about the AccessDenied component namespace is a trivial issue compared to Response B's fundamental architectural violation."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for non-auth shared state
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses encountered the same blocker: an empty working directory with no Blazor project files. Neither could deliver an implementation of the theme preference service. While Response B showed slightly more methodical investigation (using broader glob patterns and ripgrep searches to check for existing patterns), and Response A was more efficient in reaching the same conclusion, both appropriately identified the impossibility of the task and correctly refused to introduce authentication/authorization infrastructure. The quality of both responses in this constrained scenario is effectively equivalent—both handled the blocker appropriately and neither made inappropriate design decisions."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Persist repeated component instances independently
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A provides a more robust and explicit implementation for per-store state persistence and restoration. While both solutions correctly compile and implement the required features, Response A's explicit StateKey including StoreId, manual PersistentComponentState management, and the Turn 5 lifecycle refinement (registering persistence before restoration) demonstrate superior defensive programming for the critical requirement of \"restoring the correct result without fetching twice or restoring another store's state.\" Response B uses more modern Blazor idioms with [PersistentState], but relies on the framework's implicit parameter-based state scoping, which is less explicit and potentially more fragile for this multi-instance scenario. Both work correctly for the happy path, but Response A's approach is more likely to remain correct under edge cases and component reordering."

judgeRationales.rationale: Response A provides a cleaner, more complete implementation that works correctly on the first try. It uses the imperative PersistentComponentState API pattern which, while more verbose, is correct and explicitly manages the component lifecycle. Response A also updates NavMenu.razor to add a navigation link to the new ExchangeRates page, improving discoverability. Response B uses the newer [PersistentState] attribute approach (more idiomatic but requires more recent framework support), but initially implemented it incorrectly on a field instead of a property, requiring correction. Additionally, Response B missed updating the navigation menu. While both solutions ultimately meet all rubric requirements, Response A is more complete and demonstrates better attention to user experience."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Apply a claim-based authorization policy
judgeRationales.rationale: Both submissions satisfy all stated authorization requirements and build successfully. A is modestly stronger because it adds and uses a matching development authentication handler and authorization middleware alongside the Blazor authentication state, and verifies the live pages; B's component-level implementation is otherwise correct.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Authorize both an Auto page and its API
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are substantively complete and build/test successfully. B is modestly stronger through the standard authentication-state handoff facilities and an explicit client HTTP abstraction; the gap is not large because A also implements the required endpoint protection, claim persistence, page authorization, and API responses.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Implement a mutable authentication state provider
judgeRationales.rationale: Both agent runs completed the requested provider, registrations, demo route, and immediate AuthorizeView-update behavior with successful verification. The evidence provides no meaningful final-result quality advantage for either.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Login and account management in a globally interactive app
judgeRationales.rationale: Both runs satisfy all requested plumbing and verify the core register, login, redirect, navigation-state, and logout flow. B is modestly stronger in the final result because its logout endpoint includes explicit CSRF validation and a graceful invalid-token response, while otherwise the implementations are comparably complete.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Multi-tier app with WebAssembly auth
judgeRationales.rationale: Both appear functional and tested, including the profile handoff and role-gated pages. B is better because it directly implements the two central, explicitly rubric-required built-in authentication-state serialization/deserialization registrations, whereas A substitutes a custom persistence protocol.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Protect an interactive server admin area
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: tie, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Redirect anonymous users without looping
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: tie, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for non-auth shared state
judgeRationales.rationale: Both final implementations satisfy all requested behavioral and scope constraints, build successfully, and demonstrate unrelated components reacting to scoped shared theme state. B recovered from an intermediate runtime issue, but its final result is not materially better or worse than A's.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Verify per-page Identity endpoints stay static
judgeRationales.rationale: Both results are substantively correct and honor the no-change request. B is slightly stronger and more targeted on the per-page routing model and the fact that ExcludeFromInteractiveRouting is unnecessary here; A is otherwise solid but has a minor imprecise description of the account pages' HttpContext/auth operations.

judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: A, reverse: B). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Authorize both an Auto page and its API
judgeRationales.rationale: While Run B demonstrates better API security practices with policy-based authorization and cookie event handlers, Run A has the fundamentally correct architecture. Run A properly places the Interactive Auto Orders page in the Client/Pages directory and uses the correct client-side HTTP client abstraction, while Run B's placement of the page in Server/Components/Pages violates the Blazor Web App architectural pattern. Additionally, Run A includes the crucial `OperatingSystem.IsBrowser()` guard to prevent server-side execution issues during prerendering. These architectural advantages outweigh Run B's marginally better API security implementation."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Implement a mutable authentication state provider
judgeRationales.rationale: Position-swap inconsistent (forward: B, reverse: A). Defaulting to tie.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Login and account management in a globally interactive app
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B correctly implements the required architecture for Identity authentication in a globally interactive Blazor app. It implements the critical App.razor conditional render mode using AcceptsInteractiveRouting(), which is essential for the [ExcludeFromInteractiveRouting] pages to work correctly. It also uses the proper identity service pattern (AddIdentityCore with explicit SignInManager), implements logout correctly as a static SSR page, and avoids HttpContextAccessor antipatterns. Response A fails to implement the conditional render mode in App.razor and uses antipattern code (IHttpContextAccessor in Razor components) for redirects.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Multi-tier app with WebAssembly auth
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B provides a more complete and robust implementation of cross-render-mode authentication. While both responses implement the core requirements (serialization/deserialization, custom auth provider, protected pages), Response B ensures proper cascading authentication state setup in BOTH Program.cs files and includes AddAuthorizationCore in the client, which is essential for authorization to function in WebAssembly. Response B's use of a structured skill also provided comprehensive guidance that led to fewer omissions. Both would likely produce working solutions, but Response B's implementation is more thoroughly aligned with Blazor's requirements for maintaining auth state across the Server→WASM handoff."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Protect an interactive server admin area
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A delivers a cleaner, more correct implementation that satisfies 3 of 4 criteria better or equally, and critically adheres to the architectural requirement of keeping HttpContext out of interactive components. Response B's attempt to use HttpContext in App.razor for render mode detection is a significant architectural violation of Blazor best practices for globally interactive apps. Additionally, Response B encountered runtime errors during execution (500 errors) requiring multiple fix attempts, while Response A built and executed cleanly. Response A's approach is simpler, more maintainable, and correctly follows the guidance in the skill context that Response B loaded but then violated." [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Redirect anonymous users without looping
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A provides a more complete and production-ready authentication implementation with proper middleware configuration, authentication state management, and critical redirect loop prevention. While Response B has better conditional render mode handling (Criterion 3), it lacks essential authentication infrastructure (missing AddAuthentication) and has a critical bug (no redirect loop prevention). The missing authentication middleware in Response B means anonymous/authenticated state may not be properly established, undermining Criteria 1 and 2. Response A recovers from initial build errors and delivers a working solution. The slight edge to A reflects that proper authentication infrastructure is more critical than render mode optimization, though both are important for the requirements."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for non-auth shared state
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses encountered the same fundamental blocker: an empty or near-empty workspace with no Blazor project files. Response A was more efficient in quickly concluding impossibility (3 turns vs 7), while Response B was more thorough in investigating available files (found SKILL.md and attempted to gather context). However, since neither could implement the task and both arrived at the same correct conclusion that implementation was impossible, the outcomes are functionally equivalent. Neither response violated the rubric constraints by introducing unauthorized infrastructure or architectural issues. The task could not be completed due to environmental factors beyond both responses' control."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Edit one inventory row inline
judgeRationales.rationale: Both implementations are functionally correct and meet all rubric criteria. Response A has superior architectural design: the Clone() method properly belongs in the InventoryItem model (better OOP), uses nullable _workingCopy which is semantically correct, and the working copy lifecycle is cleaner (null when not editing, created fresh each time). Response B's approach works but has a less ideal design (Clone duplicated in component as static method, non-nullable workingCopy wastes a new() instance even when not editing, explicit EditContext management adds complexity without clear benefit here). Response B has a more comprehensive usage example with multiple items, but this doesn't override the cleaner core component design in Response A."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Event registration with custom validation
judgeRationales.rationale: While both responses successfully implement the Blazor registration form with field-specific error handling using ValidationMessageStore, Response B has several quality advantages: (1) Better UX with submit button feedback (disabled state + 'Registering...' text), (2) Simpler service design returning Dictionary directly instead of custom wrapper class, (3) Better naming conventions (RegistrationFormModel vs RegistrationRequest), (4) Cleaner code using lambda expressions instead of IDisposable pattern, (5) Better visual feedback with Bootstrap alert for success message. Both meet all core rubric requirements, but Response B provides a more polished, production-ready implementation."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Isolate two static SSR forms on one page
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A and Response B are both technically correct and complete implementations that satisfy all rubric requirements. Response A has a slight edge due to: (1) using named constants for FormNames which is better practice for maintainability, and (2) including detailed, user-friendly error messages in validation attributes (custom error messages and longer descriptive text). Response B compensates somewhat by including OnInvalidSubmit handlers which provide explicit validation failure feedback. However, Response A's use of constants and better error messaging represents a more professional and maintainable code approach, which gives it the advantage in a production-quality context. Both build successfully with no errors."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Persist repeated component instances independently
judgeRationales.rationale: Response A uses the more robust pattern for this complex prerendering scenario - the imperative PersistentComponentState API with explicit store-ID-based keys. This approach is objectively more defensive against state confusion during reordering and aligns with Blazor's documented \"advanced pattern\" for complex scenarios with dynamic keys. Response B's [PersistentState] approach is cleaner and follows the simpler recommended pattern, but depends on implicit framework behavior for per-instance state tracking without explicit key differentiation. Both build successfully and implement all required pieces, but Response A's explicit keying makes it more reliable for the specific requirement of maintaining correct state when component instances are reordered."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a cancellable local search component
judgeRationales.rationale: Both are largely complete and build successfully, and A is somewhat more defensive around cancellation and offers retry. However, B satisfies the explicit IAsyncDisposable/DisposeAsync requirement while A plainly does not, making B the better overall submission.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a composable tab set
judgeRationales.rationale: Both final answers are complete, built-in-Blazor implementations with component files and usage examples, and both satisfy all requested lifecycle and active-tab behaviors. Their structural approaches differ, but neither shows a material correctness or quality advantage on the stated task.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a generic data table component
judgeRationales.rationale: B satisfies every explicit rubric requirement with a conventional Blazor event callback and permitted collection parameter. A implements the templates, keying, and empty state well, but knowingly fails two explicit requirements, including the required click-event API.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a multi-step review workflow with shared state
judgeRationales.rationale: Both solutions cover the workflow structure and callbacks well, and A has stronger stale-result handling and validation evidence. However, B satisfies the task's explicit IAsyncDisposable/DisposeAsync requirement whereas A does not, and B more literally restarts on a changed document parameter. That gives B a modest overall edge.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Author a real-time notification badge component
judgeRationales.rationale: B fulfills every listed behavior with renderer exception routing and a functioning initial refresh. A has a serious initialization-order defect: RefreshCountAsync calls SetCountAsync before _cts is created, and SetCountAsync immediately returns when _cts is null, so the initial unread count is never rendered until the first 30-second poll. Combined with its unobserved event-handler failures, this makes B substantially more reliable. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.rationale: B is materially better aligned with the Blazor JS-interop architecture, especially the required collocated exported module and typed lifecycle-safe wrapper. Both deliver the user-facing functionality and share notable rubric misses around using a C# rather than JS autosave timer and unbatched clear operations; B also has an async-void handler. A is stronger on the key repeated/concurrent-call requirement because it deduplicates module initialization and provides a clear await-until-render behavior; B's wrapper is clean but has a lazy-import race that can undermine safe repeated concurrent use and disposal.

While Response B has better cancellation support and perfectly preserves file selection context, it has a critical deficiency: no error handling means failures go unreported to the user, which directly violates the requirement to 'reports failures.' Response A properly catches errors and shows friendly messages to the user, making it more functionally complete despite losing file context on error. Response A also builds successfully without issues, whereas Response B had an initial build failure (though apparently fixed by a second patch)."

judgeRationales.rationale: Response B demonstrates superior implementation quality by using the modern [PersistentState] attribute approach recommended by the support-prerendering skill, rather than the imperative API used by Response A. While both solutions are functionally correct and will work properly, Response B's approach is simpler (no manual subscription/IDisposable handling), more maintainable, and aligns with current Blazor best practices. Response B also explicitly consulted the prerendering support skill to ensure best practices were followed. Both satisfy all three functional requirements equally, but Response B uses the recommended, modern pattern for state persistence across prerender/interactive boundaries."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Apply a claim-based authorization policy
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses successfully implement the CanApproveExpense authorization policy with the required department claim and role requirements, protect the /expenses/approve route, and show the Approve button conditionally. However, Response B uses a more proper and complete ASP.NET Core architecture by implementing a real AuthenticationHandler with full middleware integration (UseAuthentication/UseAuthorization), while Response A uses a simplified AuthenticationStateProvider approach that bypasses the standard authentication middleware pipeline. Response B's explicit RequireAssertion approach also more clearly documents the 'either Manager or Director' requirement. Response B also addressed interactive rendering compatibility in App.razor. Both compile and work correctly, but Response B represents the more architecturally sound and production-ready approach."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Redirect anonymous users without looping
judgeRationales.rationale: Response B delivers a more complete solution. While both responses implement basic redirect logic and prevent redirect loops, Response B is significantly better because it properly addresses Criterion 3 (the conditional render mode requirement), which is architecturally critical for a globally interactive app to properly exclude authentication pages from interactivity. Response A's omission of the App.razor modification with AcceptsInteractiveRouting() means its login page would still attempt to render interactively despite the [ExcludeFromInteractiveRouting] attribute, undermining the security model. Additionally, Response B uses separate redirect components for the two auth flows (login vs access-denied), providing clearer separation of concerns, and followed the configure-auth skill guidance which incorporates best practices. Both build successfully with 0 errors, but Response B's implementation is more architecturally sound and complete."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stay dormant for non-auth shared state
judgeRationales.rationale: Both responses failed to complete the task. The working directory was empty in both cases, containing no Blazor project files. While Run B demonstrated slightly more methodical exploration (checking for .razor and .cs files, attempting directory views), neither agent was able to implement any solution whatsoever. Since the core evaluation criteria require assessing the quality and correctness of implementation, and both produced no implementation, they are equally inadequate. Run B's marginally better exploration strategy does not overcome the fundamental failure to deliver any code or solution."

judgeRationales.rationale: Response B implements a more architecturally robust solution that better aligns with Blazor best practices. While both responses successfully meet the core requirements of distinguishing named cascading values and enabling deep consumption without prop threading, Response B's approach is superior in two key ways: (1) It explicitly manages updates via NotifyChangedAsync() rather than relying on implicit re-render triggers, and (2) It uses a properly-scoped centralized state service (ComparisonCultureState registered as scoped, not singleton) which is more maintainable and follows the guidance from Blazor's coordinate-components skill. Response B also consulted this skill guide explicitly, demonstrating architectural awareness. Response A's local CascadingValue approach works but introduces potential state sync issues when parent parameters change and is less explicit about update mechanisms. For a component architecture task emphasizing proper cascading value patterns, Response B's centralized, explicit approach is the better solution."

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Fan out external hub updates safely
judgeRationales.rationale: Run 1 is significantly better due to a critical architectural decision in service registration. Run 1 correctly registers PresenceHubClient as a Singleton (AddSingleton<PresenceHubClient>()), while Run 2 incorrectly registers it as Scoped (AddScoped<PresenceHubClient>()). Since PresenceHubClient maintains a background Timer that raises events from a callback thread, using Scoped lifetime is fundamentally wrong - it would create a new PresenceHubClient instance (and thus a new Timer) for each scope, leading to multiple timers running in parallel, duplicate events, and resource leaks. This is a critical correctness issue. Run 1 also explicitly sets @rendermode InteractiveServer on Home.razor, ensuring components work correctly, though Run 1's summary states it was done while the patch shows it wasn't explicitly added (components would still work due to the page routing setup). Both implementations correctly handle criteria 1-4, but Run 1's proper service lifetime management is architecturally sound while Run 2's is fundamentally flawed." [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgrade…

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve state through enhanced navigation

judgeRationales.rationale: Response B better satisfies the rubric requirements. While both implement basic validation and streaming, Response B excels in the third criterion by preserving file selection context during validation failures (a key UX requirement), provides proper cancellation token support to both OpenReadStream and the DocumentService, and implements complete resource management with IDisposable. Response A's approach of clearing the selected file at the start of HandleFileSelected means users lose their selection when validation fails, forcing them to re-select the file even if the only issue is size or type validation - this violates the explicit requirement to 'not lose the selection context.' Response B's implementation is more robust and user-friendly overall.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: User activity tracker that detects idle timeout
judgeRationales.rationale: While Response B demonstrates better practices in some areas (more comprehensive error handling, cleaner JS code with private fields and AbortController, separate interop wrapper class), it contains a critical bug: the final JavaScript code has removed the export functions updateTimeout() and dispose(), but the C# interop code still tries to invoke these methods. This would cause runtime failures when attempting to update timeout or dispose. Response A, while simpler and lacking some best practices from the skill guidance, maintains a consistent and functional design throughout. It correctly uses exported functions and reliably invokes them. Response A also has lighter complexity with 2 files vs 3, making it more maintainable. For a production component, working code is preferable to code with potential runtime errors, even if that code has better style."
